newsitem.title: USA: Death toll rises as U.S. hurricane downgraded.
newsitem.headline: Death toll rises as U.S. hurricane downgraded.

text.p: Hurricane Fran was downgraded to a tropical storm early on Friday after causing extensive damage in North and South Carolina where at least 11 people died in weather-related incidents.

The National Hurricane Centre in Miami said that at 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT) Fran had winds of about 65 mph (100 kph) and was now a tropical storm. It continued to weaken as it moved inland, the Miami-based centre said.

On Thursday, Hurricane Fran smashed into the Carolina coast packing winds of up to 120 mph (193 kph) snapped power lines, tossed trees into houses and cut off power to hundreds of thousands of people.

At 5 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Friday, the storm was centred about 25 miles (40 km) north northwest of Raleigh, North Carolina. As the storm marched further inland, forecasters said there were fears heavy rains would cause severe flooding.
There was also a possibility of isolated tornadoes over parts of eastern North Carolina and central and southeastern Virginia, forecasters said.
At least 11 deaths have been linked to the powerful hurricane, according to news reports.
Tom Ditt, a spokesman for the North Carolina emergency management team, told CNN there had been nine deaths in his state. Two more were killed in South Carolina as a result of the storm.
Two people were killed south of Raleigh when their vehicle struck a tree that had fallen across a highway, Frank Cope, public information officer for Wake county in North Carolina, told Reuters.
In North Carolina's Onslow county, an 18-year-old woman died on Thursday night when a tree toppled by hurricane-force winds fell onto her mobile home, emergency officials said.

Two people were killed in Johnston county when a tree fell on their home and a Durham county fireman was killed responding to an emergency call, said a spokesman for North Carolina's emergency management team.
In South Carolina, an elderly woman died on a rain-slicked highway when she lost control of her car and crashed into a tree, the state highway patrol said.
North Carolina Governor Jim Hunt said the hurricane had caused "very serious damage" in his state.

"There are 5-10 feet (1.524 metres to 3.048 metres) of water on some of those roads right on the coast," Hunt said from the state's emergency management centre. "There are a lot of trees down and power is out in many, many counties.

In the small North Carolina town of Southport, officials also said damage had been severe. "We've got a lot of destruction," said Steve Robbins, a Southport Police Department dispatcher. "There are a lot of buildings down, demolished. It's really bad down here.
"It was almost like a movie," Robbins said, when the eye passed over the small town. "The whole city was black. It was like a horror movie."
In Raleigh damage was extensive from fallen trees and high winds. "Things are so bad we are urging people not to even go to shelters anymore because of the fallen trees," said Cope.
All along the coast of North and South Carolina, nuclear power reactors were shut, shops and bridges closed and homes boarded up as people waited out the storm.
About 200,000 residents evacuated low-lying areas and sought refuge in motels, stayed with friends or went to Red Cross shelters.

In South Carolina, which missed the worst of Fran's force, at least 58,700 customers had no power in the Myrtle Beach area. An additional 10,000 homes on the beach area known as "the Grand Strand" were also left in the dark after palm trees felled power lines.
South Carolina officials said the state could lose about $8 million a day in tourist revenue because of the hurricane.
